description: We are a creative and technology-driven collective of developers and engineers passionate about technology, space exploration, and building innovative solutions. We are driven by the challenge of transforming ideas and complex data into accessible, useful digital tools with real-world impact.
summary: We built a public web tool to see how the sky changes in SPHEREx infrared images and discover moving objects, no expertise required. Users enter RA/Dec, a field of view and one of the 102 spectral bands; the system queries NASA/IPAC IRSA, downloads real FITS cutouts from different epochs and plays them as an animated sequence, with zoom, coordinates, side-by-side comparison and GIF export. A scientific engine aligns and subtracts consecutive epochs, looking for the bright/dark pair that reveals a shift, rejects fixed stars, and returns for each candidate its position, displacement, motion (″/yr) and signal-to-noise ratio. A hunter mode lets users mark an object by hand in every epoch, and a field guide teaches how to tell real movers from false positives. The interface is bilingual and every view can be shared by URL. This matters because SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months and no single team can sift through that much data alone: making the science understandable lets the public take part in real discoveries.
details:
What it does and how it works

This public explorer lets anyone hunt for asteroids, brown dwarfs, and nearby stars across all 102 near-infrared channels (0.75–5 µm) of NASA’s SPHEREx mission. When a user enters sky coordinates, an instant astrophysical pipeline masks bad pixels, aligns multi-epoch frames onto a shared celestial grid (WCS), and computes the temporal median of the cube (mean if n < 3) to define the still sky S. Subtracting this background yields the residual Rᵢ = Iᵢ − S, where fixed stars and zodiacal light cancel out and only movers remain. The engine then smooths the first and last residuals (σ = 1.2 px), isolates real peaks (SNR > 3.8), and pairs displacements (1.2 < Δpix < 70) to calculate proper motion μ = Δθ/Δt (arcsec yr⁻¹). Results appear immediately with blink, swipe, hunter mode, GIF export, a 3.3 µm methane (CH₄) teaching signature, and live catalog cross-matches.

Data access

The system requests multi-epoch sky cutouts from the IRSA archive (currently addressing SPHEREx Quick Release 2) with a strict 3.5 s timeout so the interface never stalls. When visits are returned, the astronomical arrays are processed directly without writing heavy files; if the archive times out or the field is empty, the engine automatically synthesizes a five-epoch sky cube (with a six-month cadence and injected moving targets) so alignment, residual imaging, and the interactive viewer always remain demonstrable.

Astrometric alignment 

Observations are sorted chronologically by Modified Julian Date (MJD) and mathematically reprojected onto the celestial coordinate grid (WCS) of the first usable visit, while saturated and flagged sensor pixels are masked out.

Static-sky cancellation 

Following the approach of WiseView and NEOSSat, the still reference sky S is defined as the temporal median of the multi-epoch cube (or the mean if n < 3). Subtracting this reference yields the residual frame Rᵢ = Iᵢ − S, where fixed stars and zodiacal light cancel out and only moving objects remain.

Motion detection

We apply Gaussian smoothing (σ = 1.2 px) to the first and last residual frames, isolate peaks with SNR > 3.8, and pair candidates showing plausible displacements (1.2 < Δpix < 70). Pixel separation is converted into arcseconds on the reference WCS to compute proper motion μ = Δθ/Δt (arcsec yr⁻¹), retaining the 15 highest-SNR tracks and interpolating their positions across intermediate epochs.

Delivery

Each epoch is delivered North-up in two views (original and residual) inside an interactive explorer featuring blink, swipe, hunter mode, GIF export, a live 102-band spectral slider, and a WiseView-style shareable link that preserves coordinates and display settings. It also provides an optional 102-channel spectral plot displaying a 3.3 µm methane (CH₄) absorption dip (generated as a teaching signature), instant cross-matching against Gaia DR3 high-proper-motion stars and IMCCE SkyBoT asteroids, and curated presets (WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, ε Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis).

Benefits

We turn massive, inaccessible telescope archives into immediate visual understanding. Instead of handling raw scientific files, users get a time-lapse sky movie, a residual toggle (Rᵢ = Iᵢ − S) that erases static stars so moving targets shine clearly, and a table of the top 15 candidates (position, displacement, proper motion μ, and SNR) overlaid with Gaia and SkyBoT data to instantly separate known bodies from potential new discoveries.

Intended impact

Because SPHEREx remaps the entire sky every six months, no small team can visually inspect a billion sources by hand. By embedding coordinates and display settings into a shareable web link, our tool lets anyone apply the exact blink method that discovered Pluto—comparing two dates to spot what jumps—bringing citizen science directly into astronomical discovery.

Tools

We integrated astronomical coordinate projection, statistical image processing, and animation tools into a bilingual (Spanish/English) interface that runs on any standard device without special hardware. The platform connects directly to NASA’s infrared archive (IPAC/IRSA), the European Space Agency’s Gaia DR3 star catalog, and the IMCCE SkyBoT asteroid database.

Creativity

We turned SPHEREx into a live blink comparator featuring a 102-band infrared slider (0.75–5 µm), an interactive measurement reticle (Hunter mode), WiseView-style shareable links, and curated celestial presets (like Barnard’s Star and WISE 0855). Built-in scientific pedagogy includes an interactive Pluto discovery story, a visual guide to spot instrumental artifacts (cosmic rays, ghosts, variables, and dipoles), and a 3.3 µm methane (CH₄) absorption curve showing how infrared light reveals cold worlds.

Factors we considered

We balanced five core priorities: uninterrupted responsiveness (a 3.5 s archive timeout backed by a synthesized five-epoch sky cube so the tool never stalls), visual lightness (delivering clean images instead of heavy files), seamless catalog verification, scientific honesty (relying on transparent median residuals Rᵢ = Iᵢ − S and first-vs-last epoch pairing rather than overclaiming complex orbital fits), and a frictionless single-search workflow.
